small_guidance:
- The N=8192 dimension is reduced via LogSumExp, so partial tiles along N create a two-pass design with extra memory traffic. Add wider BLOCK_N configs (e.g. 256/512) and bias toward fewer N-tiles to reduce the second-pass overhead; with M=1024, BLOCK_M=128–256 keeps the grid healthy.
- Add `triton.Config({'BLOCK_M': 128, 'BLOCK_N': 256, 'BLOCK_K': 64}, num_warps=8, num_stages=4)` and `BLOCK_M=256, BLOCK_N=128, BLOCK_K=64` variants; large K=8192 benefits from BLOCK_K=64 with num_stages=4 to better overlap loads.
- Pre-transpose W to [K, N] once in `__init__` (store as a buffer) so the inner load becomes contiguous along N, enabling vectorized loads and removing strided W access in the K loop.
large_guidance:
- Use a split-K / persistent design: one program per row-block of M that streams the full N=8192 dimension in chunks, maintaining an online (running-max, running-sumexp) LogSumExp accumulator in registers. This eliminates the partial buffer + second kernel entirely and fuses all activations into a single epilogue store of shape [M,1].
- Alternatively, keep the two-pass GEMM but make the first kernel write only per-row (max, sumexp) by performing an in-kernel reduction across all N tiles via atomics or a persistent-grid scheme keyed on row-tile; the finalize kernel is then trivial M element-wise ops fused with the GEMM tail.
- Cache W transposed ([K,N] contiguous) at module init so the matmul becomes a standard A@W layout with coalesced N-major loads; combined with BLOCK_N≥128 this should push closer to peak FP32 bandwidth on the 4090.
